extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, computer scientists, and formal-methods practitioners writing non-trivial proofs (authors of mathematical proofs and users of proof assistants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing hierarchical, numbered, machine-checker-friendly mathematical proofs (Lamport-style structured proofs) that make dependencies, hypotheses, quantifiers, and case splits explicit and easy to re-check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number every step
rubrics_metrics.description: Every step in the proof is numbered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a hierarchical numbering scheme so each assertion has a unique label (e.g., ⟨1⟩1, ⟨1⟩2, ⟨2⟩1). Numbering clarifies structure, allows precise references, and prevents ambiguity about which assertion a sentence belongs to.

rubrics_metrics.name: State what each step proves
rubrics_metrics.description: Every step states what it proves — the label should indicate the assertion that the step establishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each numbered step should be labeled with the exact assertion it proves (not merely a vague comment). This makes dependencies explicit and supports top-down or bottom-up checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make 'obvious' leaves verifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminal 'obvious' steps (leaves) must be short enough that an attentive reader cannot disagree with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is designated 'obvious' it should be small and directly checkable; avoid accumulating many large 'obvious' claims because a single false one can invalidate the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly state hypotheses in force
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypotheses currently in force at each step must be explicit; assumptions are stated, not assumed from context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on ambient context to imply which assumptions apply. For each step, list or make clear the hypotheses used so a reader (or a mechanical checker) can verify correctness locally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit quantifiers and case splits
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantifiers and case splits must be made explicit in the proof structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ambiguous scope for quantifiers and hidden case distinctions. Introduce explicit subproofs for each case and explicitly bind quantifiers so dependencies and scopes are unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name the Q.E.D. at each level
rubrics_metrics.description: The Q.E.D. at each level should be named to tell the reader which assertion has been established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminate subproofs with a Q.E.D. that references the assertion proven (e.g., 'Q.E.D. (proves ⟨1⟩2)'). This documents the conclusion of the subproof and makes checking easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof re-checkable top-down or bottom-up
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof should be structured so it can be re-checked either top-down or bottom-up independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A properly structured proof allows a reader to verify that each step follows from its children (bottom-up) or that children suffice to prove the parent (top-down). This property aids human checking and mechanization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured-proof node rule (tree form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each proof is a tree: each node is a numbered step labeled with the assertion it proves and is either a terminal 'obvious' step or has a sub-proof whose conjunction of children implies the parent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write proofs as hierarchical trees where nonterminal nodes have explicit subproof lists. Use the convention that a parent is justified when its listed children collectively imply it. Example notation given by Lamport (with hierarchical labels ⟨i⟩j).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make dependency graph explicit (avoid prose hiding structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid prose constructions ('since … and … so') that obscure which assertions depend on which; make the dependency graph explicit in the structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of chaining consequences in running text, place each consequence in its own numbered step and reference precisely which earlier statements are used. This prevents hidden dependencies and makes the logic checkable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep case structure explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure proofs by cases preserve and display the case structure explicitly in the hierarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create separate subproofs for each case and label them clearly. Do not tuck different cases into flowing prose where the reader may lose which statements belong to which case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make quantifier scope unambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly indicate the scope of quantifiers so there is no ambiguity about which variables and quantifiers are in force at each step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the quantifier bindings where they take effect and use the hierarchical structure to show where quantified assumptions hold; this reduces mistakes arising from implicit scopes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer structured proofs for non-trivial proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the structured-proof format primarily for non-trivial proofs where errors are likely; very short or very famous simple proofs may not need structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamport concedes that trivial or widely-known short proofs (e.g., infinitude of primes) don't require full structuring. Reserve the method for proofs where clarity and error-detection matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate prose proofs with mechanical checkers
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 21st-century approach, the prose proof should be the same artifact as the formal proof used by mechanical checkers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure proofs to be machine-checker friendly (Isar/Lean-style blocks). Aim for proofs that can be both read as human-oriented prose and verified by a proof assistant, reducing divergence between informal and formal arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use electronic usability features (hyperlinks, collapsible subproofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: For electronic proofs, provide hyperlinked references and collapsible sub-proofs to aid navigation and comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link numbered steps so readers can jump to referenced assertions; allow collapsing of subproofs in interfaces to reduce visual complexity while retaining explicit structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical benefit: structured proofs reduce hidden errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Structured proofs tend to expose errors that prose conceals; Lamport observed higher bug-detection rates when proofs were rewritten in structured form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this empirical observation as justification for structuring non-trivial proofs and for integrating with formal verification workflows; track 'bug rate' if doing systematic verification to measure effectiveness.
